analysis.title: US Power Pipeline: September capacity additions accelerate, led by solar and storage
key_insights: Net US generation capacity rose 5.6 GW in September 2026, the strongest September in 10 years versus a 1.5 GW historical September average. Solar added 3.0 GW and battery storage 1.6 GW.
Capacity added through September equals 60% of GS's 2026 net addition estimate, versus a 59% average since 2020. Year-to-date, storage is at 92% of the full-year estimate, wind 88% and solar 51%.
Natural gas simple-cycle added 675 MW in September, bringing YTD additions to 23% of the full-year forecast. CCGT stayed at 37% with no September additions.
No coal retirements were recorded for a fifth consecutive month, leaving YTD retirements at 46% of GS's 3.7 GW full-year forecast.
The 2027 solar pipeline rose to 105% of GS's net addition estimate from 103% in the August data. Wind was 107% versus 108%. The 2028 solar pipeline rose to 77% from 72%, with wind unchanged at 58%.

Renewable pipeline coverage falls sharply in 2029-2030 (solar 41% and 13%, wind 36% and 5% of GS estimates). GS says this may reflect shorter development timelines or uncertainty around tax credit sunsets.

Natural gas pipeline coverage is concentrated in 2028-2030 at 116%, 111% and 155% of GS's expected additions. The 2028 and 2029 figures rose from 101% and 103% in the August data. 17 GW of projects, including 12 GW from Fermi America, were added to the pipeline in the March EIA release.

GS sees labor availability as a key and tightening constraint on power build-out. NextEra said on its Q1 2026 call that labor is the single biggest constraint on new gas generation, citing EPC contractors falling from 9-11 to four and competition from LNG terminals and data centers. Argan, Primoris and Quanta flagged shortages of CCGT project managers and linemen.

GS estimates the US power industry needs more than 500,000 new workers by 2030: about 300K across manufacturing, construction and operations plus about 207K in transmission and distribution. Even with all energy apprenticeships deployed to T&D, a 78K gap remains in the base case, which closes if apprenticeships rise from ~45K to ~65K a year from 2027.

Transmission and distribution equipment is supply constrained: large power transformers quote 3-4 year deliveries and switchgear 1-2 years. GS's Korea power equipment analysts see skilled labor as one of the biggest constraints on production ramp.
It can take 8 years to develop a worker with 5 years of experience, so new labor supply will be slow even as electrical trade school enrollments rise (up 400% in some regions).
Solar pipeline is 122 GW. 44% of planned capacity (60 GW) has faced delays of 6+ months, down from a 53% peak in September 2024. 7.3 GW was postponed or canceled YTD in 2026.
Wind pipeline is 20 GW (down 6.72 GW y/y). 52% of planned capacity has faced 6+ month delays, up from 27% in Nov 2023. No cancellations in the trailing twelve months.
Natural gas pipeline is 71 GW (up 30.54 GW y/y). 11.6% of planned capacity has faced 6+ month delays, versus a 47.3% peak in December 2022.
Energy storage pipeline is 64 GW. 39.2% of planned capacity has faced 6+ month delays, down from a 55.5% peak in December 2023. 6.3 GW was postponed or canceled YTD in 2026.

GS is constructive on renewables-exposed names (NXT, XEL, FSLR; NEE Not Rated) and highlights PWR as a beneficiary of labor constraints given its scale in labor access. The note underpins a 3.5% CAGR in US power demand through 2030.

market_movers.rationale: Beneficiary of robust renewable capacity additions. On the Conviction List (CL). Target based on 22x P/E on Q5-Q8 EPS forecasts.
Constructive on renewable build-out exposure. Target applies 19.5x to Q5-Q8 earnings forecasts.
Benefits from renewable additions. Target is 10.0x ex-cash P/E on Q5-Q8 EPS with about $16 per share of net cash added back.
Accelerating labor constraints should benefit EPC companies with scale in labor access. Target based on 26.0x NTM EV/EBITDA.
Not Rated, but should benefit given high renewables exposure. GS is advising on an announced strategic matter involving NextEra.

sector_views.rationale: Robust renewable capacity additions and a supportive EIA pipeline through 2027 reinforce the constructive view on renewables-exposed names.
Labor tightness favors contractors with scale in labor access.

earnings_insights: NextEra management said on its Q1 2026 earnings call that labor is the single biggest constraint on new gas generation build-out.
Quanta Services said on its FY2025 earnings call that data center labor is tight and transmission linemen are likely to be tight in the second half of 2026.
Argan cited availability of project managers for CCGT work as a key focus. Primoris cited linemen availability in its Power Delivery business.

macro_indicators.interpretation: GS's forecast for power demand growth, driven partly by AI and data center deployment, underpins the capacity and labor analysis.
Earlier GS estimate used to model a net increase of about 510K US power and grid jobs.

macro_indicators.indicator: US net generation capacity change, September 2026
macro_indicators.interpretation: Strongest September in 10 years, from EIA data.

trade_ideas.description: Long PWR (Buy, $781 target) as a beneficiary of labor constraints in power build-out
trade_ideas.rationale: Signs of accelerating labor constraints should benefit EPC companies with scale in labor access.
trade_ideas.risk: Slower revenue CAGR from loss of project volume momentum, delays from supply chain challenges, slower margin progression from cost inflation or operational challenges.

trade_ideas.description: Long renewables-exposed names NXT, XEL and FSLR (Buy rated)
trade_ideas.rationale: Robust renewable capacity additions reinforce the constructive view.
trade_ideas.risk: FSLR: module oversupply, higher module costs, trade policy, US manufacturing credit changes. XEL: negative rate cases, litigation, ROE gap, cost management.

risk_factors: Skilled labor shortages could pose a significant risk to project execution across the power value chain.
EIA project updates are self-reported by developers and subject to changes in timing and execution.
Renewables pipeline declines meaningfully in 2029-2030, which may reflect tax credit sunset uncertainty.
Long delivery times for large power transformers (3-4 years) and switchgear (1-2 years).
FSLR: module oversupply, higher module costs, trade policy, changes to US manufacturing credits.
XEL: negative rate case outcomes, litigation, gap between earned and authorized ROE, cost management.
PWR: slower revenue growth, supply chain delays, cost inflation.
charts_described: Exhibit 4 plots net capacity change in September for the past 10 years, with September 2026 at 5.6 GW versus a 1.5 GW 10-year average.
Exhibit 5 shows capacity added through September as a share of the full year, with the 6-year average at 59% versus 60% for 2026.
Exhibit 1 compares planned solar, wind and gas capacity to GS estimated net additions for 2027-2030, with solar at 105%, 77%, 41% and 13%.
